turns.response_html:
The stovetop in your photo is a traditional electric coil cooktop. The style you are looking for—a flat, completely sealed top that still relies on electric resistance heating underneath—is known as a solid disk element (or solid surface element).

Are they standard sizes?

Yes, electric cooktop burners are highly standardized across North America. They almost always come in two standard nominal sizes:

  • 6-inch diameter for small burners
  • 8-inch diameter for large burners

Can you buy conversion elements?

While you can find individual solid disk replacement elements, they are generally manufactured as direct OEM repair parts for stoves that already came with a solid disk setup.

True plug-and-play conversion kits that allow you to simply unplug your open coil element and plug in a solid cast-iron disk (like retrofits manufactured by brands like SmartBurner or ENCON Euro-Burner) do exist online, but they have become increasingly rare and specialized over time.

Important Considerations Before Upgrading

If you do locate solid disk retrofit elements online or at a specialized local appliance parts store, keep a few trade-offs in mind:

  • Heating and Cooling Time: Cast iron solid disks take significantly longer to heat up and cool down than open wire coils.
  • Cookware Requirements: Solid disks require completely flat-bottomed cookware to transfer heat efficiently. If your pans are warped, cooking will be very uneven.
  • Alternative Option: If you are looking to eliminate the grease-trapping holes entirely, many people choose to replace the entire cooktop appliance with a smooth ceramic glass radiant cooktop or an induction cooktop, both of which feature a completely seamless, easy-to-wipe flat surface.

turns.prompt_text: I've got two more questions. The first one is I imagine these stove tops work through high current and not high voltage but I'm not sure And I'm also not sure how much it matters or if it's the wasp that matter here The other question is what if I just put some sort of thin metal plate over the top essentially and maybe bonded it to the steel resistive spiral?
turns.response_html:
Your instincts about how these stovetops handle electricity are spot on. Let's break down the physics of what's happening under the pan, and then look at why adding a custom metal plate is a recipe for trouble.

1. Voltage vs. Current (and the Power That Matters)

When it comes to heating your food, it's the total wattage (the power) that matters most. However, the way the appliance achieves that wattage relies on a specific balance of voltage and current.

In standard North American appliances, an electric stove plugs into a heavy-duty 240V outlet (unlike standard 120V wall outlets).

  • The Math: Electric power ($P$, measured in watts) is the product of voltage ($V$) and current ($I$, measured in amps): $$P = V \times I$$
  • High Current vs. High Voltage: Because the voltage is fixed at 240V, a large burner pulling 2,400 watts requires a current of 10 amps. While 240V is higher than a standard wall outlet, it isn't "high voltage" in an industrial sense (like power lines). However, 10 to 15 amps is a substantial amount of current flowing through a circuit.
  • Resistance is the Key: The burner coil is essentially a massive, insulated resistor. According to Joule's First Law, the heat generated is proportional to the square of the current multiplied by the electrical resistance ($R$): $$P = I^2 \times R$$

So, to answer your question: The watts (total power) are what actually cooks your food. To get those high watts safely, the stove utilizes a moderately high voltage (240V) so that the current (amps) stays at a manageable level that household wiring can handle without overheating.

2. Placing a Metal Plate Over the Coil

It is incredibly tempting to just drop a flat piece of sheet metal over the coils to create a DIY smooth-top. However, bonding or placing a metal plate directly over an open coil element is highly dangerous and will likely destroy the stovetop for a few reasons:

The Air Gap Trap

No matter how flat the plate is, it will not perfectly match the warping of the coil as it heats up. You will trap thin pockets of air between the coil and the plate. Air is an excellent thermal insulator. The heat will get trapped in the coil, causing it to rapidly overheat and burn out its internal core.

Thermal Expansion and Bonding Failure

If you try to bond a plate to the coil (using a high-temperature adhesive or brazing), the two different metals will expand and contract at completely different rates when heating up to temperatures over 500°C (932°F). This mechanical stress will quickly crack the bond, warp the plate, or snap the coil itself.

Safety Risks

Altering the burner changes how heat radiates away from the element. This can easily cause the reflective drip pans underneath to overheat, potentially damaging the internal wiring of the stove or creating a fire hazard.

If you want the benefits of a flat surface without replacing the whole stove, a safer temporary alternative is using a standalone, heavy-duty cast iron griddle that sits securely on top of the elements when you cook, though you'll still have to deal with cleaning the spills that make it past the edges.
